xs-internals(7) ​

How it works

The local engine, the remote exchange and the life of one file, with the source files behind each.

OVERVIEW ​

xs is one executable with three roles. As a local engine it copies between two paths on one machine. As a client it starts xs --server on another machine over ssh and plays the sender (push) or the receiver (pull). As that helper it plays the other role. All three share the same scanner, the same receiver-side generator and the same file writer. Parallelism comes from a worker pool with two queues: one for scanning and comparing directories, one for moving file data (src/pool.h).

LOCAL ENGINE ​

  • Scan. Directories are listed by a pool of threads. On macOS, getattrlistbulk returns names and attributes in one call per directory. On Linux, each entry is a readdir plus an fstatat, and backlog F-06 tracks a faster path (src/fs.cpp, src/local.cpp).
  • Generator. Source and destination listings are merge-joined per directory, and each entry is checked against the filters, case and Unicode name collisions (src/names.cpp), and the requested metadata. Every write goes through a directory file descriptor and never follows a symlink inside the destination (src/destination.cpp).
  • Clones. On one APFS volume with at least -pt, a new directory that holds only files and symlinks is cloned in a single call, and other files are cloned one by one. -X, -U, -N, --chmod, --chown, --fileflags, -S and --bwlimit turn whole-directory clones off, because they need per-entry handling.
  • Deletion runs before, during, or after transfer, depending on --delete-WHEN. It is skipped entirely when the source had I/O errors, unless --ignore-errors is given.

REMOTE EXCHANGE ​

  • Pipelining. The sender does not wait for the full file list. Each directory’s listing goes out as soon as it is scanned, and the receiver answers per directory, so data starts flowing while most of the tree is still being walked.
  • Blocks. Files up to 512 KiB are packed together into blocks of about 1 MiB, so thousands of small files cost a few large writes on the wire. With -z, each block is compressed with zstd and decompressed on several threads. Every block carries an XXH3 checksum (src/remote.cpp).
  • Acknowledged progress. On a push, the progress bar follows what the receiver reports as written, not what was sent, so it cannot reach 100% before the data has landed.
  • One stream. Everything shares one ssh connection, so on a fast LAN the ssh cipher can become the limit before the disks do (backlog F-03).

The frames are listed in the protocol reference.

THE LIFE OF ONE FILE ​

  • Resume. With --partial, both sides hash an existing destination prefix with XXH3-128. If the hashes match, only the remaining bytes are sent. The receiver re-checks the prefix while copying it, so a prefix that changes meanwhile fails rather than producing mixed data (src/remote.cpp, src/local.cpp).
  • Delta. For changed files over 1 MiB, a rolling weak checksum finds candidate blocks in the existing file, and XXH3 confirms them. The sender then sends block references and literal data. The matcher keeps one block plus 1 MiB of source data in memory, and the rebuilt file is checked as a whole before it is published (src/delta.cpp).
  • Source changes. A source file that changes while it is being read is detected, and a delta transfer retries once. A file that still cannot be read consistently is reported as an error (exit 23) and not published.
  • Interruption. On Ctrl-C, a timeout or a closed output pipe, temporary files are removed. With --partial, the completed contiguous prefix is kept for the next run.

Where each part lives. The full list of source files and tests is on the contributing page.
